fetched_contents.text: Congenital heart defects in children born after assisted reproductive technology: a CoNARTaS study Abstract Background and Aims Children born after assisted reproductive technology (ART) have worse perinatal outcomes compared with spontaneously conceived children. This study investigates whether children conceived after ART have a higher risk of congenital heart defects (CHDs) compared with children born after spontaneous conception (SC). Methods All 7 747 637 liveborn children in Denmark (1994–2014), Finland (1990–2014), Norway (1984–2015), and Sweden (1987–2015), where 171 735 children were conceived after ART, were included. National ART and medical birth registry data were cross-linked with data from other health and population registries. Outcomes were major CHDs, severe CHDs, 6 hierarchical CHD lesion groups, and 10 selected major CHDs, diagnosed prenatally or up to 1 year of age (Denmark, Finland, and Sweden) and prenatally or at birth (Norway). The association between ART and CHDs was assessed with multivariable logistic regression analysis, with adjustment for available confounders. Results Major CHDs were detected in 3159 children born after ART (1.84%) and in 86 824 children born after SC [1.15%; adjusted odds ratio (AOR) 1.36; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.31–1.41]. Risk was highest in multiples, regardless of conception method. Severe CHDs were detected in 594 children born after ART (0.35%) and in 19 375 children born after SC (0.26%; AOR 1.30; 95% CI 1.20–1.42). Risk was similar between ICSI and IVF and between frozen and fresh embryo transfer. Conclusions Assisted reproductive technology–conceived children have a higher prevalence of major CHDs, being rare, but severe conditions. The absolute risks are, however, modest and partly associated with multiple pregnancies, more prevalent in ART. Auger et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae549. Many systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and large observational studies show an association between ART and low birth weight (LBW) and preterm birth (PTB). Although multiple births are the most important cause of the increased risk of PTB and LBW in ART-conceived children compared with children born after spontaneous conception, risk of these outcomes is also higher in ART-conceived singletons.5–8 Several meta-analyses and original studies have found that birth defects are more common in children born after ART compared with children born after spontaneous conception. Estimates of excess risk range between 30% and 70%.7–10 A systematic review, including 29 studies, by Qin et al.7 reported birth defects in 5.7% [95% confidence interval (CI) 4.7%–6.9%] of singletons born after in vitro fertilization (IVF)/intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) and in 3.9% (95% CI 3.1%–4.8%) of singletons born after spontaneous conception. Most studies show no difference in the frequency of birth defects in children born after IVF vs. ICSI, nor in children born after fresh vs. frozen-thawed embryo transfer (FET).10,11 The increased rate of birth defects found among children born after ART could partly be explained by parental subfertility according to a recent study from Australia.12 Congenital heart defects (CHDs) refer to structural anomalies of the heart and the intrathoracic vessels present during pregnancy or at birth.13 Congenital heart defects are the most commonly occurring birth defects, accounting for ∼50% of all major birth defects, affecting ∼1%–2% of children in the general population.14–17 Although many CHDs are recorded at birth and a few later in life, the true incidence of CHDs remains largely unknown due to lack of identification in pregnancies ending in miscarriages, terminations, or stillbirths.13,18,19 Heart defects are a major paediatric health concern and remain the leading cause of mortality from birth defects.20 Several systematic reviews and cohort studies have found an increased risk of CHDs in children born after ART.21–23 A recent review including 41 cohort and case–control studies with 25 856 children born after ART showed an increased risk of CHDs in the ART-conceived group as compared with spontaneous conception [SC; pooled odds ratio (OR) 1.45; 95% CI 1.20–1.76].21 Congenital heart defects are more common in twins compared with singletons,24,25 and a recent study found that most of the association between ART and CHD was mediated by twinning.26 For specific CHDs, conflicting results have been reported.21,27 Using nationwide data from four Nordic countries, we assessed the risk of major CHDs in ART-conceived liveborn children compared with children born after spontaneous conception. fetched_contents.text: Congenital Heart Diseases: Recent Insights into Epigenetic Mechanisms Abstract Congenital Heart Diseases (CHDs) are a heterogeneous group of structural abnormalities affecting the heart and major arteries, which are present in at least 1% of births worldwide. Studies have linked CHD to both genetic and environmental factors. In this regard, it has been demonstrated that changes in the epigenetic pattern impact the expression of key genes involved in proper cardiac development. Therefore, it is suggested that aberrant epigenetic mechanisms may contribute to the development of these pathologies. Here, we review and summarize the main epigenetic mechanisms involved in CHD. Moreover, cardiac development and the importance of the environment and CHD are also addressed. Keywords: congenital heart diseases, epigenetics, DNA methylation, histone modifications, polycomb and trithorax protein complexes, non-coding RNAs 1. Introduction Epigenetics is the field that studies the structural modifications that occur in the genome and modulate gene expression without altering the nucleotide sequence. These modifications are driven by diverse mechanisms, among which DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs stand out. All are key in regulating gene expression and accessibility [1]. In this framework, alterations of epigenetic modifications impact several cardiac structures, promoting the manifestation of a wide range of irregular phenotypes, such as Congenital Heart Diseases (CHDs). This term encompasses a set of heterogeneous structural anomalies that jeopardize the heart and the major arteries [2]. These cardiac structural alterations are present in at least 1% of births worldwide [3], with the highest incidence reported in Europe and North America (9.4 per 1000 live births) [4]. The classification of CHD has been performed in several ways in the past. The report of the guidelines for the management of adults (AHA/ACC 2018) with Congenital Heart Disease does so according to their anatomy and physiological complexity [5]. From this point of view, simple or non-complex defects include those that can be treated without surgery, such as ventricular and atrial septal defects (VSDs, ASDs), respectively, or defects like Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA); meanwhile, complex and critical defects require immediate medical attention and surgery during the first year of life, as is the case with Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), Ebstein anomaly (EA) or Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS) [6]. From a clinical and often more convenient standpoint, these pathologies can also be divided between cyanotic and non-cyanotic. The first kind are characterized by a right-to-left shunt resulting in cyanosis and include conditions such as TOF, Tricuspid Atresia (TA) and transposition of the great arteries (TGA), while the second kind can be obstructive, like Pulmonary Stenosis (PS) or Coarctation of the Aorta (CoA) [7]. It has been shown that changes in epigenetic signatures have a direct impact on key genes involved in heart development. For example, hypermethylation of the TBX20 gene has been identified in patients with TOF, ASD, and VSD, suggesting an anomalous epigenetic regulation that may contribute to the development of these pathologies [8,9]. Likewise, non-coding RNAs take on crucial roles in heart development, as seen, for example, with the downregulation of miR-1, which is associated with impaired differentiation of embryonic stem cells (ESCs) towards cardiomyocytes, highlighting the importance of microRNAs (miRNAs) for the adequate formation of cardiac tissue [10]. This evidence supports a role for epigenetic modifications as determinants in the occurrence and progression of CHD, directly impacting key cardiac anatomic structures, such as the heart valves, the atrial or ventricular walls, and the major arteries [11]. Intrinsically, cardiac embryology is determined by interactions with the environment, mainly through hemodynamic signaling, which leaves the embryo vulnerable to anomalous development in response to external hemodynamic stimuli but also gives it a high degree of adaptability, which explains the limited spectrum of viable phenotypes up until birth. The multiple and complex levels of gene regulation make it difficult to unravel the precise epigenetic mechanisms involved in CHD. Currently, the use of genomic technologies that allow for the identification of a wide range of genetic defects, like Third-Generation Sequencing (TGS) and Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWASs), has allowed for significant progress in the field of genomic medicine. Particularly, TGS involves wide and high-quality reads, permitting the better comprehension of genomic structure and avoiding previous amplification by PCR. This technique has already been applied in several studies involving genetic diseases, and recently it has been applied to genome assembly, structural variant detection, epigenetic analysis, and pharmacogenomics (PGx) profiling studies [12,13]. Furthermore, GWASs represent a fundamental tool for identifying genetic variants associated with complex diseases and other relevant phenotypes. These studies include wide arrays of individuals. At the moment, the use of GWASs has positively impacted research into multifactorial illnesses, identifying new robust associations of several alleles influencing disease phenotypes in a highly reproducible manner [14,15]. The arrival of these tools has therefore enhanced research into the genetics and epigenetics of CHDs, making them essential for advancing research in this field. Therefore, the early detection of epigenetic marks associated with CHD is crucial for better prevention and the possibility of personalized therapeutic approaches that benefit patients. Here, we review and summarize the role of the epigenetic mechanisms involved in CHD. 2. Mini-report on specific CHD subtypes and their reported associations with ART

The evidence provided here supports a general pattern that ART is associated with an increased risk of congenital heart defects overall, but the data are uneven for specific subtypes. For the most common septal defects, the evidence is strongest for atrial septal defect (ASD) and ventricular septal defect (VSD), while evidence for tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is more sparse and less consistently reported. For hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) and transposition of the great arteries (TGA), the evidence is primarily background and descriptive rather than directly causal, and the studies cited here do not establish a consistent ART association.

Ventricular septal defects and atrial septal defects:  
The strongest direct evidence for septal defects comes from the general ART-CHD literature. The CoNARTaS study found that ART-conceived children had higher prevalence of major CHDs overall, and it explicitly noted that the literature shows conflicting results for specific CHDs [N2-F1]. The excerpt also describes ASD and VSD as common congenital heart defects, but it does not report a specific ART risk estimate for either one [N4-R4]. A broader source in the search results similarly frames ASD and VSD as common types of congenital heart defects, but again without a direct ART-specific risk figure [N4-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports that septal defects are among the most common CHD subtypes, but the current ART literature does not establish a uniformly strong or consistent association for either ASD or VSD [N2-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Tetralogy of Fallot:  
The evidence is more limited for TOF. The CoNARTaS study mentions that specific CHD associations are conflicting and that the study explored whether any specific CHD was increased in ART-conceived children [N2-F1]. A separate review excerpt notes that TOF is a complex and critical CHD and is among the anatomical categories used to classify congenital heart defects [N6-F3]. However, the search evidence provided does not include a direct ART-to-TOF study or a consistent risk estimate for TOF. So, for TOF, the current evidence supports its classification as a major CHD, but it does not establish a strong, consistent ART association [N6-F3][N2-F1].

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome and transposition of the great arteries:  
For HLHS and TGA, the evidence here is mainly background and observational rather than directly causal. The search results include studies on prenatal diagnosis and outcomes for these conditions, but none of them establish an ART-specific risk estimate [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The CoNARTaS study does not report HLHS or TGA separately as a major finding, and the search excerpts do not show a direct link between ART and either condition [N2-F1][N3-R1]. Therefore, the evidence supports that these are serious CHD subtypes, but it does not show a consistently reported ART association [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-F3].

Septal defects and other septal-related abnormalities:  
The evidence suggests that septal defects are a broad category of CHD, including ASD and VSD, but the provided material does not provide a consistent ART-specific risk estimate for all septal-related abnormalities. The CoNARTaS study found higher overall CHD risk in ART-conceived children, and the search excerpts describe ASD and VSD as common defects, but they do not report specific ART odds for septal defects as a group [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence therefore points to septal defects as a clinically important subgroup, but the current ART literature is not sufficiently detailed to conclude a single strong association for all septal abnormalities [N4-R1][N4-R4].

Bottom line:  
The provided evidence is strongest for general CHD risk and weaker for specific subtypes. ASD and VSD appear most commonly discussed, but the evidence does not support a uniformly strong or consistent ART association for either. TOF is a major CHD, but the current evidence does not establish a strong ART link. HLHS and TGA are serious CHD subtypes, but the search evidence here does not show a consistent ART association. Septal defects are an important subgroup, but the current evidence is not enough to determine whether they are the most consistently reported specific ART-related defects [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4][N6-F3][N3-R1].

Mini-report on non-CHD cardiovascular defects and broader cardiovascular outcomes

The evidence provided here indicates that ART is associated with several cardiovascular defects beyond congenital heart disease (CHD), and that these defects often overlap with CHD in terms of embryonic origins and clinical presentation. However, the evidence also suggests that cardiovascular outcomes beyond birth are less well established and may be influenced by study design and confounding.

Patent ductus arteriosus and aortic coarctation:  
The evidence directly links these defects to congenital heart disease. The CoNARTaS study reports that ART-conceived children had higher prevalence of major CHDs overall, and the search excerpts describe ASD, VSD, and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) as defects involving the wall or vessels of the heart [N2-F1][N4-R4]. A separate source in the search results explicitly states that congenital cardiac defects such as coarctation of the aorta (CoA) or PDA are ideally diagnosed and treated in early childhood, and it notes that the most commonly associated clinically significant defects include PDA, VSD, and aortic stenosis [N5-R5]. This suggests that PDA and CoA are part of the broader cardiovascular defect spectrum that overlaps with CHD, rather than being entirely distinct categories. However, the provided evidence does not report a specific ART risk estimate for PDA or CoA beyond the general CHD finding [N5-R1][N5-R5].

Overlap with and difference from CHD:  
The evidence shows substantial overlap between cardiovascular defects and CHD. The CoNARTaS study explicitly defines CHDs as structural anomalies of the heart and intrathoracic vessels present during pregnancy or at birth [N2-F1]. The search excerpts similarly describe ASD, VSD, and PDA as structural heart defects or vessel-related defects [N4-R4][N5-R5]. At the same time, the evidence also distinguishes cardiovascular defects more broadly from CHD. For example, the CoNARTaS study includes major CHDs and severe CHDs as outcomes, while the broader cardiovascular defect literature includes PDA, CoA, and other vascular anomalies [N2-F1][N5-R1]. The overlap is therefore both conceptual and clinical: many cardiovascular defects fall within the broader category of CHD, but some studies may also examine non-CHD vascular or circulatory anomalies. The evidence provided here does not clarify whether all cardiovascular defects in ART offspring are CHD or whether some are separate anomalies, so that distinction remains partly uncertain [N2-F1][N5-R1].

Later cardiovascular outcomes beyond birth:  
The evidence provided is more suggestive than definitive. The CoNARTaS study focuses on liveborn children and congenital defects diagnosed prenatally or up to 1 year of age, with no later cardiovascular outcome reported in the excerpts [N2-F1]. A separate search result mentions cardiovascular disease (CVD) in offspring conceived using ART, but this is a broader statement and does not provide specific evidence for later cardiovascular outcomes in the current wave’s cited sources [N8-R3]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that ART may be associated with later cardiovascular risk, but the current search materials do not establish a direct link to adult cardiovascular disease or long-term outcomes [N8-R3]. In other words, the evidence is consistent with cardiovascular sequelae, but the provided sources do not support a strong conclusion about later cardiovascular outcomes beyond birth [N2-F1][N8-R3].

Bottom line:  
The provided evidence indicates that ART is associated with several cardiovascular defects, including PDA and CoA, which often overlap with CHD in their embryonic origin and clinical presentation. However, the evidence does not provide a specific ART risk estimate for these defects beyond the general CHD finding, and it is not sufficient to conclude a strong association with later cardiovascular outcomes beyond birth [N2-F1][N4-R4][N5-R1][N5-R5][N8-R3].

Mini-report on mechanistic hypotheses and biological plausibility

The evidence provided here supports several mechanistic hypotheses linking ART to congenital heart disease, particularly oxidative stress, epigenetic changes, and placental factors. However, the evidence is largely observational and therefore limited in its ability to prove causation.

Main proposed mechanisms:  
The strongest mechanistic hypothesis is epigenetic dysregulation. The review excerpt states that changes in the epigenetic pattern impact the expression of key genes involved in proper cardiac development and that aberrant epigenetic mechanisms may contribute to the development of congenital heart diseases [N6-F3]. It also identifies DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs as central epigenetic mechanisms [N6-F3]. Another search result similarly describes congenital heart disease as linked to both genetic and environmental factors, with epigenetic changes affecting gene expression without altering the nucleotide sequence [N6-R2]. In addition, the evidence points to oxidative stress and placental factors as plausible contributors. One source notes that exposure to air pollutants can induce an inflammatory response and increase oxidative stress, which might alter placental circulation and affect fetal oxygenation [N6-R1]. Another source states that placental dysregulation alters nutrient transfer and impairs fetal ATP production, which may affect organogenesis, particularly cardiac and cerebral development [N6-R3]. A further source notes that optimal oxygenation of the fetal unit requires regulated placental invasion and low-resistance, high-surface vasculature [N6-R4]. Together, these mechanisms suggest that ART-related stressors may disrupt placental function, oxidative balance, and fetal cardiac development [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].

Supporting evidence from animal or human studies:  
The provided evidence includes both human observational studies and human genetics/review evidence, but no direct animal experiments are explicitly cited. The CoNARTaS study is a large observational registry-based study showing higher prevalence of major CHDs in ART-conceived children [N2-F1]. Another source reports that maternal nutritional epigenetics may affect cardiac development and that fetal epigenetic programming is susceptible to key dietary factors during the periconceptional period [N6-R5]. This supports the idea that environmental exposures and nutrition can influence epigenetic programming and cardiac development. The CoNARTaS study is observational and registry-based, which can introduce confounding and residual bias [N2-F1]. The same study adjusts for available confounders, but it cannot eliminate all confounding factors [N2-F1]. The evidence also indicates that results vary by study; some show strong associations, while others report conflicting results for specific CHDs [N2-F1][N7-R1]. These limitations suggest that the observed associations should be interpreted cautiously, and that subgroup differences may reflect true biological variation as much as methodological heterogeneity [N2-F1][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R4].

## Bottom line

Current studies report that ART is associated with an increased risk of major congenital heart defects overall, with the strongest evidence for major and severe CHDs [N2-F1]. For specific subtypes, the evidence is stronger for general septal defects and weaker or less consistent for TOF, HLHS, and TGA [N2-F1][N3-R1][N6-F3]. The evidence also suggests that ART may be associated with broader cardiovascular defects such as PDA and CoA, but the provided sources do not establish a strong specific ART risk estimate for these defects beyond the general CHD finding [N2-F1][N5-R5]. Mechanistic hypotheses point to epigenetic changes, oxidative stress, and placental factors, but observational evidence limits causal inference [N6-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3][N7-R1]. Finally, subgroup differences and study design strongly affect observed risk estimates, with multiple pregnancies, maternal age, and male infertility being important confounders [N2-F1][N7-R1][N7-R3].
